conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling since your baby arrived. We’ll be using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—often called the EPDS. It’s a short, 10-question tool that helps us understand how you’ve been coping emotionally over the past seven days. Everything you share is confidential, and this is a judgment-free space. When we’re done, we’ll talk through what your answers mean and what support might be helpful. Ready to begin?

First, in the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

I... I can still laugh sometimes, but it feels like a lot more work than it used to. Like, if my partner makes a joke or the baby does something silly, I’ll smile, but it fades quickly. Mostly I’m just tired and worried, so finding the “funny side” doesn’t come naturally right now.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not very often. I’ll give a little chuckle if something is really obvious, but even that feels forced. Most of the time I’m too worn-out or anxious to find things funny.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but now it all feels kind of “why bother.” I still do them, but it’s like I’m just going through the motions, not actually looking forward to anything.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… that happens a lot. If the baby’s fussy or won’t settle, my head jumps straight to “I’m doing something wrong” or “I’m a bad mom.” I know, logically, babies just cry, but I still end up feeling like it’s my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yes, pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly think, “What if she stops breathing?” or I’ll lie down and my heart’s racing about nothing I can name. There’s no real reason—it just shows up and sits on my chest until I distract myself.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes, that’s been happening. Sometimes it hits out of nowhere—like my heart starts racing and I feel like I can’t catch my breath. I’ll check on the baby, check the monitor, pace around the house… but nothing’s actually wrong. It just feels like something awful is about to happen, even though I can’t explain why.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes, most of the time. Between the night feedings, the laundry pile, and just trying to keep her content, I feel like I’m drowning a lot of days. I manage to get the basics done, but it’s like I’m constantly one step behind and ready to cry.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes. I lie down exhausted, but my head won’t stop spinning—going over everything I might have done wrong, worrying she’ll wake up any second. I finally drift off, then I’m up again when she makes the tiniest noise. It’s like I can’t turn the “mom switch” off long enough to rest.
I have felt sad or miserable
Yeah... most days I feel just down. I’ll be holding her and tears come out of nowhere—like I’m happy she’s here, but I still feel this heavy sadness I can’t shake.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
Yes, that’s been happening. I’ll put her in the crib, walk to the kitchen, and suddenly I’m sobbing over nothing I can name. It’s like the sadness just spills out before I even realize it’s there.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… I haven’t had any thoughts like that. I feel overwhelmed and sad, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself.

You've shared how the past weeks have felt heavy and joyless-laughing feels forced, activities you once anticipated now seem pointless, and waves of anxiety or sudden tears arrive without warning. Despite loving your baby, you describe feeling <quote>down most days</quote>, unable to rest even when exhausted, and constantly second-guessing yourself as a mom. These feelings are understandably overwhelming, and you deserve support that eases this load.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports laughing only occasionally and describes it as forced, aligning with "Definitely not so much now".</sym>, <sym>Patient reports almost total loss of anticipatory pleasure, describing activities as pointless and performed without enjoyment, aligning with "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports blaming herself "a lot" and feeling like a "bad mom" whenever the baby fusses, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Yes, very often'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden intense panic episodes with racing heart and breathlessness that occur without identifiable cause, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient says 'most of the time' and describes feeling 'drowning,' 'constantly one step behind and ready to cry,' indicating inability to cope at all.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly racing thoughts, persistent worry, and being easily woken, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports feeling sad "most days" with frequent crying spells, aligning with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, unexpected crying spells that feel uncontrollable, aligning with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS total of 26 far exceeds the ≥14 threshold indicating high probability of <med>major postpartum depression</med>. The pattern aligns with DSM-5 criteria for <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: nearly every day low mood (Q8, Q9 scored 3), diminished interest or pleasure (Q2 score 3), inappropriate guilt (Q3 score 3), psychomotor agitation suggested by pacing and racing heart (Q4, Q5 scored 3), fatigue and feeling overwhelmed (Q6 score 3), insomnia (Q7 score 3), and clinically significant distress/impairment. Anxiety symptoms coexist, a common perinatal presentation. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> this week
2. Discuss starting evidence-based treatment (therapy such as CBT or IPT, and consider antidepressant medication if recommended)
3. Plan daily low-pressure self-care: 20-minute walk outside, balanced snacks every 3-4 hours while awake, and accept help with night feeds to gain 3-4 hours of uninterrupted sleep
4. Share Edinburgh results and symptom list with a trusted support person so they can help monitor changes
5. Keep emergency numbers handy: 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline or local 24-hr crisis service, and go to ER if you ever feel unsafe with your thoughts
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Date: [today]

Patient: 4–6 weeks post-delivery, self-referred for mood assessment.

1. Endorsed symptoms (≥ 6 on EPDS analog)
   • Marked anhedonia, inability to look forward to activities  
   • Daily low mood, spontaneous crying  
   • Sleep disturbance (initial insomnia, hyper-arousal)  
   • Excessive self-blame/guilt re parenting competence  
   • Persistent, unprovoked anxiety, panic episodes  
   • Feeling overwhelmed, “drowning” in routine tasks  
   • No self-harm ideation (endorsed item 10 negative)

2. Pattern
   Consistent with moderate-to-severe postpartum depressive symptoms with comorbid anxiety; no psychotic or suicidal features reported.

3. Screening significance
   Elevated risk for major postpartum depression ± anxiety disorder; functional impairment evident (sleep, caregiving, ADLs). Score suggests benefit from formal diagnostic evaluation and possible evidence-based intervention.

4. Safety note
   Denies self-harm thoughts; no protective concerns voiced. Continue routine monitoring for emergent safety issues.

Plan: Refer for expedited clinical interview (PHQ-9, GAD-7, EPDS) and differential diagnosis; educate on emergency contacts if symptoms escalate.
